items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species"?
items.answer: variation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of variation.

items.stem: Herring gulls and lesser black-backed gulls coexist in Britain without interbreeding, yet are linked by interbreeding populations around the Arctic. This example illustrates
options: the difficulty of defining species boundaries in ring species
items.answer: the difficulty of defining species boundaries in ring species
items.markingKey: B. Gradual change around the ring blurs species limits.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the difficulties of applying the biological species concept.
items.answer: It cannot be applied to asexual organisms or fossils; it is hard to test interbreeding in geographically separated populations; hybrids are sometimes fertile; populations may be partly isolated (ring species), so boundaries are fuzzy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It cannot be applied to asexual organisms or fossils; it is hard to test interbreeding in geographically separated populations; hybrids are sometimes fertile; populations may be partly isolated (ring species), so boundaries are fuzzy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Organisms that look alike must belong to the same species." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Cryptic species look alike but do not interbreed; species are defined by reproductive isolation in the biological concept, not only appearance.
items.markingKey: Cryptic species look alike but do not interbreed; species are defined by reproductive isolation in the biological concept, not only appearance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Cytochrome c is a protein of 104 amino acids found in the electron transport chain of all aerobic organisms. The table shows the number of amino acid differences between human cytochrome c and that of other species.

Species | Amino acid differences from human | % difference
chimpanzee | 0 | 0.0
chicken | 13 | 12.5
rattlesnake | 14 | 13.5
tuna | 21 | 20.2
yeast | 44 | ?

(a) Identify the species most closely related to humans according to these data. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage difference for yeast. [2]
(c) Explain why cytochrome c is useful for comparing distantly related species. [2]
items.answer: (a) chimpanzee (b) 42.3 % (c) It is found in all aerobic organisms (universal), has an essential function so changes slowly, so differences accumulate gradually over very long times.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] chimpanzee (A1). (b) [2] 44/104 × 100 (M1) = 42.3 % (A1). (c) [2] Present in all aerobic organisms (A1); slow, steady rate of change (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The biological species concept is the most useful way to define a species."
items.answer: It is the most useful concept for sexually reproducing living organisms, but biologists need several complementary concepts (morphological, phylogenetic) for other cases.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is based on the evolutionary process of reproductive isolation that separates gene pools; it explains why species remain distinct when they live together. Arguments against: it cannot be used for asexual organisms, fossils or allopatric populations; hybridisation with fertile offspring occurs in many plants and some animals. Supported judgement: It is the most useful concept for sexually reproducing living organisms, but biologists need several complementary concepts (morphological, phylogenetic) for other cases.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hybrid"?
options: A cell or organism with two sets of chromosomes (2n), one from each parent
The number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position
The differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species
The offspring of a cross between two different species, often infertile
items.answer: The offspring of a cross between two different species, often infertile
items.markingKey: D. "hybrid" is the offspring of a cross between two different species, often infertile.

items.stem: Distinguish between chromosome number differences between species and variation within a species.
items.answer: Different species often have different chromosome numbers (e.g. chimpanzee 48, human 46), contributing to reproductive isolation; within a species chromosome number is normally constant and variation is due to differences in alleles.
items.markingKey: Different species often have different chromosome numbers (e.g. chimpanzee 48, human 46), contributing to reproductive isolation; within a species chromosome number is normally constant and variation is due to differences in alleles. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lions and tigers can produce “ligers” in captivity, but they never interbreed in the wild. Which statement is best supported?
options: They are separate species, though the boundary is not absolute.
Ligers prove they belong to one genus only.
items.answer: They are separate species, though the boundary is not absolute.
items.markingKey: A. Potential interbreeding in captivity shows limitations of the biological species concept.

items.stem: With reference to the ring of Ensatina salamanders around the Central Valley of California, explain how it illustrates the limitations of the biological species concept.
items.answer: Neighbouring populations interbreed, but the two end populations in the south coexist without interbreeding. Speciation is gradual, so there may be no clear point at which populations become separate species.
items.markingKey: Context (Neighbouring populations interbreed, but the two end populations in the south coexist without interbreeding.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Speciation is gradual, so there may be no clear point at which populations become separate species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limitations of the biological species concept.

items.stem:
The table shows the diploid chromosome number, haploid genome size and approximate number of protein-coding genes for several eukaryotes.

Species | Diploid number | Genome size / billion base pairs | Protein-coding genes
dog (Canis familiaris) | 78 | 2.4 | 19 000
bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) | 42 | 16 | 107 000
rice (Oryza sativa) | 24 | 0.43 | 38 000
fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) | 8 | 0.14 | 14 000
horse (Equus caballus) | 64 | 2.5 | 20 000

(a) Identify the species with the largest genome. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times larger the genome of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is than that of fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). [2]
(c) Calculate the number of genes per million base pairs for the species with the smallest genome. [2]
(d) Using the data, evaluate the claim that more complex organisms have larger genomes. [3]
items.answer: (a) bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) (b) 114 times (c) 100 genes per Mb (d) Not supported: genome size does not follow complexity – e.g. bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) has the largest genome; gene number is also not proportional to genome size; most large genomes contain much non-coding/repetitive DNA.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) (A1). (b) [2] 16/0.14 (M1) = 114 (A1). (c) [2] 14000 ÷ (0.14 × 1000 Mb) (M1) = 100 (A1). (d) [3] Claim not supported (A1); specific comparison from data (A1); explanation – non-coding DNA / polyploidy (R1).

items.stem: A karyogram is used to deduce which of the following?
options: the blood group of a person
the base sequence of every gene
the sex of an individual and the presence of chromosome abnormalities such as trisomy
items.answer: the sex of an individual and the presence of chromosome abnormalities such as trisomy
items.markingKey: C. XX/XY and an extra chromosome 21 are visible.

items.stem: Amara writes: "The largest genomes belong to the most complex animals." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some plants (e.g. Paris japonica, 149 Gb) and amoebae have far larger genomes than humans; most of the difference is non-coding DNA.
items.markingKey: Some plants (e.g. Paris japonica, 149 Gb) and amoebae have far larger genomes than humans; most of the difference is non-coding DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a genome and a karyotype.
items.answer: A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA.
items.markingKey: A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Hybrids can be produced between two species of zebra with diploid numbers 32 and 34. State the chromosome number of the hybrid and explain why it is likely to be infertile.
items.answer: 33; chromosomes cannot all pair as homologues in meiosis, so gametes are unbalanced
items.markingKey: 16 + 17 = 33 (A1); chromosomes from different species are not homologous / odd or unmatched set cannot pair in meiosis I (R1); gametes have incomplete sets (R1).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Human Genome Project (1990–2003) and explain what it reveals about the use of whole-genome sequencing.
items.answer: An international project sequenced about 3 billion base pairs and estimated about 20 000 protein-coding genes. It provided a reference genome for comparing individuals and species, and the cost of sequencing has since fallen from billions of dollars to a few hundred.
items.markingKey: Context (An international project sequenced about 3 billion base pairs and estimated about 20 000 protein-coding genes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It provided a reference genome for comparing individuals and species, and the cost of sequencing has since fallen from billions of dollars to a few hundred. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of whole-genome sequencing.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Whole-genome sequencing of every newborn baby should become routine."
items.answer: Targeted screening offers clear benefits now; routine whole-genome sequencing needs strong safeguards and better interpretation of variants before it is justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it could detect genetic diseases early and guide treatment; costs have fallen dramatically. Arguments against: it raises issues of privacy, consent and possible discrimination; most variants are of uncertain significance and may cause anxiety. Supported judgement: Targeted screening offers clear benefits now; routine whole-genome sequencing needs strong safeguards and better interpretation of variants before it is justified.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "karyotype"?
options: Determining the complete base sequence of all the DNA of an organism
A branching diagram showing the evolutionary relationships within a clade, based on shared derived characteristics or sequence data
The number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position
DNA shed by organisms into their surroundings (water, soil, air) that can be collected and sequenced to identify which species are present
items.answer: The number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position
items.markingKey: C. "karyotype" is the number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position.

items.stem: Human chromosome 2 has two inactive centromere-like regions and telomere sequences near its middle. What does this suggest?
options: It formed by fusion of two ancestral chromosomes that remain separate in other great apes.
items.answer: It formed by fusion of two ancestral chromosomes that remain separate in other great apes.
items.markingKey: C. This explains 46 vs 48 chromosomes.

items.stem: A karyogram shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. What is the correct interpretation?
items.answer: a female with Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
items.markingKey: C. Two X = female; extra 21 = trisomy 21.

items.stem: Using the Human Genome Project (1990–2003) as an example, explain the use of whole-genome sequencing.
items.answer: An international project sequenced about 3 billion base pairs and estimated about 20 000 protein-coding genes. It provided a reference genome for comparing individuals and species, and the cost of sequencing has since fallen from billions of dollars to a few hundred.
items.markingKey: Context (An international project sequenced about 3 billion base pairs and estimated about 20 000 protein-coding genes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It provided a reference genome for comparing individuals and species, and the cost of sequencing has since fallen from billions of dollars to a few hundred. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of whole-genome sequencing.

items.stem: Compare the genomes and karyotypes of different species and discuss what such comparisons reveal.
items.answer: Chromosome numbers vary (human 46, chimp 48, dog 78); fusion of chromosome 2; genome size varies widely (yeast 12 Mb, human 3.1 Gb, Paris japonica 149 Gb) and does not correlate with complexity or gene number; sequence comparison reveals relationships and common ancestry; human–chimp 98–99 % similarity; uses in classification.
items.markingKey: Chromosome numbers vary (human 46, chimp 48, dog 78); fusion of chromosome 2; genome size varies widely (yeast 12 Mb, human 3.1 Gb, Paris japonica 149 Gb) and does not correlate with complexity or gene number; sequence comparison reveals relationships and common ancestry; human–chimp 98–99 % similarity; uses in classification.

items.stem: What is an advantage of eDNA surveys over traditional surveys?
items.answer: species can be detected without seeing or capturing them
items.markingKey: species can be detected without seeing or capturing them. Rare or elusive species leave DNA traces.

items.stem: "A dichotomous key can use as many choices as needed at each step." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A dichotomous key always offers exactly two contrasting choices at each step.
items.markingKey: A dichotomous key always offers exactly two contrasting choices at each step. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the use of eDNA to track invasive Asian carp in the Great Lakes shows the benefits and limitations of eDNA.
items.answer: Carp DNA was detected beyond barriers, prompting further monitoring. It gives early warning of invasions but positive results may come from boats or birds carrying DNA, not live fish.
items.markingKey: Context (Carp DNA was detected beyond barriers, prompting further monitoring.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It gives early warning of invasions but positive results may come from boats or birds carrying DNA, not live fish. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the benefits and limitations of eDNA.

items.stem: A dichotomous key is needed for 12 invertebrate species collected from leaf litter. State the number of couplets needed and suggest two features suitable for the first couplets.
items.answer: 11 couplets; e.g. number of legs (6, 8, many/none); presence of segments; presence of a shell; wings present/absent.
items.markingKey: 11 couplets; e.g. number of legs (6, 8, many/none); presence of segments; presence of a shell; wings present/absent.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "eDNA will soon make traditional field identification skills unnecessary."
items.answer: eDNA is a powerful complement, but field identification remains essential to validate results, build databases and study populations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: eDNA can detect many species quickly and cheaply, including rare and cryptic ones; metabarcoding can survey whole communities from one sample. Arguments against: eDNA gives little information on abundance, behaviour, condition or life stage; reference databases rely on specimens identified by trained taxonomists. Supported judgement: eDNA is a powerful complement, but field identification remains essential to validate results, build databases and study populations.

items.stem: Explain how a dichotomous key is used to identify an organism.
items.answer: Starting at the first couplet, the user chooses which of two contrasting descriptions fits the specimen; each choice leads to another numbered couplet or a name; this is repeated until the organism is identified.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Starting at the first couplet, the user chooses which of two contrasting descriptions fits the specimen; each choice leads to another numbered couplet or a name; this is repeated until the organism is identified. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Researchers sequence water from a river in Borneo and find DNA matching an otter species never recorded there. What should they do before publishing?
options: Confirm with repeat samples and controls to rule out contamination, and ideally a camera trap.
items.answer: Confirm with repeat samples and controls to rule out contamination, and ideally a camera trap.
items.markingKey: B. Verification is essential in eDNA work.

items.stem: Describe how species can be identified using dichotomous keys and environmental DNA, and evaluate each method.
items.answer: Key: paired contrasting features, n − 1 couplets, observable stable characters, specimen needed; strengths: cheap, in the field; limits: expertise, variation, life stages. eDNA: sample, filter, extract, PCR barcode, sequence, database; strengths: non-invasive, rare species, many species; limits: degradation, contamination, abundance unknown, database gaps.
items.markingKey: Key: paired contrasting features, n − 1 couplets, observable stable characters, specimen needed; strengths: cheap, in the field; limits: expertise, variation, life stages. eDNA: sample, filter, extract, PCR barcode, sequence, database; strengths: non-invasive, rare species, many species; limits: degradation, contamination, abundance unknown, database gaps.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "taxon"?
options: The use of the rate at which mutations accumulate in a gene or protein to estimate the time since two lineages diverged
Simultaneous identification of many species in a mixed sample by sequencing barcode regions of all the DNA it contains
An identification tool made of a series of paired, mutually exclusive descriptions, each leading to another pair or to the name of an organism
A group of organisms at any level of the classification hierarchy, such as a genus or family
items.answer: A group of organisms at any level of the classification hierarchy, such as a genus or family
items.markingKey: D. "taxon" is a group of organisms at any level of the classification hierarchy, such as a genus or family.

items.stem: "Organisms in the same order are more closely related than those in the same genus." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The genus is a lower, more specific taxon; members of a genus are more closely related than members of an order.
items.markingKey: The genus is a lower, more specific taxon; members of a genus are more closely related than members of an order. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain the evidence that led to the three-domain classification.
items.answer: Woese compared base sequences of ribosomal RNA, which is present in all cells and evolves slowly; prokaryotes fell into two groups as different from each other as from eukaryotes; supported by differences in membrane lipids, cell walls, histones and RNA polymerase. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Woese compared base sequences of ribosomal RNA, which is present in all cells and evolves slowly; prokaryotes fell into two groups as different from each other as from eukaryotes; supported by differences in membrane lipids, cell walls, histones and RNA polymerase. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Organisms living in hot acidic springs have prokaryotic cells, no peptidoglycan, ether-linked membrane lipids and histone-like proteins. To which domain do they belong?
items.answer: Archaea
items.markingKey: A. Ether lipids and no peptidoglycan indicate Archaea.

items.stem: Using Carl Woese’s analysis of 16S ribosomal RNA (1977) as an example, explain the three-domain system of classification.
items.answer: Methanogens had rRNA sequences very different from both bacteria and eukaryotes. The data led to Archaea being recognised as a separate domain, changing the highest level of classification.
items.markingKey: Context (Methanogens had rRNA sequences very different from both bacteria and eukaryotes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The data led to Archaea being recognised as a separate domain, changing the highest level of classification. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the three-domain system of classification.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The Linnaean hierarchy of ranks is no longer useful in modern biology."
items.answer: Ranks remain useful as a communication tool, but classification should be based on clades revealed by molecular evidence; the hierarchy is a convention, not a natural law.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ranks (e.g. class, order) are arbitrary and not equivalent across groups; cladistics focuses on clades rather than ranks. Arguments against: ranks provide a familiar framework for communication and teaching; binomial names and genera remain essential for identification and conservation. Supported judgement: Ranks remain useful as a communication tool, but classification should be based on clades revealed by molecular evidence; the hierarchy is a convention, not a natural law.

items.stem: Which domain includes fungi, plants and animals?
items.answer: Eukarya
items.markingKey: D. All organisms with nucleated cells.

items.stem: Which statement about a natural classification is correct?
options: It allows prediction of characteristics shared by members of a group.
It is based only on habitat.
items.answer: It allows prediction of characteristics shared by members of a group.
items.markingKey: A. Shared ancestry implies shared traits.

items.stem:
The table shows the diploid chromosome number, haploid genome size and approximate number of protein-coding genes for several eukaryotes.

Species | Diploid number | Genome size / billion base pairs | Protein-coding genes
horse (Equus caballus) | 64 | 2.5 | 20 000
bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) | 42 | 16 | 107 000
donkey (Equus asinus) | 62 | 2.4 | 20 000
human (Homo sapiens) | 46 | 3.1 | 20 000
fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) | 8 | 0.14 | 14 000

(a) Identify the species with the largest genome. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times larger the genome of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is than that of fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). [2]
(c) Calculate the number of genes per million base pairs for the species with the smallest genome. [2]
items.answer: (a) bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) (b) 114 times (c) 100 genes per Mb

items.stem: Describe the classification hierarchy and explain why the three-domain system replaced earlier classifications.
items.answer: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; example (e.g. human: Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens). Earlier two-kingdom/five-kingdom systems based on morphology; Woese rRNA: Archaea distinct; Archaea vs Bacteria lipids, walls, histones; reflects evolutionary relationships; natural classification predictive.
items.markingKey: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; example (e.g. human: Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens). Earlier two-kingdom/five-kingdom systems based on morphology; Woese rRNA: Archaea distinct; Archaea vs Bacteria lipids, walls, histones; reflects evolutionary relationships; natural classification predictive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "molecular clock"?
options: Simultaneous identification of many species in a mixed sample by sequencing barcode regions of all the DNA it contains
A chain of neighbouring populations that can interbreed, whose end populations cannot, making species boundaries unclear
The science of naming, describing and classifying organisms
The use of the rate at which mutations accumulate in a gene or protein to estimate the time since two lineages diverged
items.answer: The use of the rate at which mutations accumulate in a gene or protein to estimate the time since two lineages diverged
items.markingKey: D. "molecular clock" is the use of the rate at which mutations accumulate in a gene or protein to estimate the time since two lineages diverged.

items.stem: Distinguish between a traditional taxonomic group and a clade.
items.answer: A clade includes a common ancestor and all its descendants, defined by shared derived features or sequences; traditional groups may be based on overall similarity and can exclude some descendants (e.g. reptiles without birds).
items.markingKey: A clade includes a common ancestor and all its descendants, defined by shared derived features or sequences; traditional groups may be based on overall similarity and can exclude some descendants (e.g. reptiles without birds). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Isabel writes: "A cladogram shows which species evolved from which present-day species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Present-day species are at the tips; a cladogram shows common ancestors (nodes), not that one living species evolved from another.
items.markingKey: Present-day species are at the tips; a cladogram shows common ancestors (nodes), not that one living species evolved from another. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the placement of whales within the even-toed ungulates (Cetartiodactyla), explain how it illustrates cladistics using molecular and morphological evidence.
items.answer: DNA sequences and fossil ankle bones show whales share a common ancestor with hippopotamuses. Sequence data revealed a relationship not obvious from body form, which fossils then confirmed.
items.markingKey: Context (DNA sequences and fossil ankle bones show whales share a common ancestor with hippopotamuses.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Sequence data revealed a relationship not obvious from body form, which fossils then confirmed. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cladistics using molecular and morphological evidence.

items.stem: The haemoglobin β-chain gene of two species of oak differs at 12 positions. Calibration with dated fossils shows that this gene accumulates differences between two lineages at 1.5 per million years. Estimate how long ago the two lineages diverged.
items.answer: 8.00 million years ago
items.markingKey: Time = differences ÷ rate = 12 ÷ 1.5 (M1) = 8.00 Myr (A1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Molecular data should always take priority over morphological data when constructing cladograms."
items.answer: Molecular evidence is usually more reliable for living organisms, but the strongest cladograms combine molecular and morphological evidence, especially to include fossils.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sequences provide thousands of characters and are less affected by convergence; molecular data resolved relationships such as whales with hippos. Arguments against: DNA cannot be obtained from most fossils, so morphology is needed for extinct species; different genes can give conflicting trees, and horizontal gene transfer complicates analysis. Supported judgement: Molecular evidence is usually more reliable for living organisms, but the strongest cladograms combine molecular and morphological evidence, especially to include fossils.

items.stem: Explain the assumptions and limitations of the molecular clock.
items.answer: It assumes mutations accumulate at a constant rate; rates differ between genes, lineages and over time; selection can speed or slow change; it must be calibrated with fossils of known age, so estimates have uncertainty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It assumes mutations accumulate at a constant rate; rates differ between genes, lineages and over time; selection can speed or slow change; it must be calibrated with fossils of known age, so estimates have uncertainty. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Birds and crocodiles share a more recent common ancestor than crocodiles and lizards. What does this mean for the group “reptiles” excluding birds?
options: Birds are not related to reptiles.
It is not a clade (it is paraphyletic).
items.answer: It is not a clade (it is paraphyletic).
items.markingKey: B. A clade must include all descendants.

items.stem:
Part of a homologous gene was sequenced in three species:
species R: ACGAACGAGCTACTCAGT
species S: ACGAACGCGCTACTCAGT
species P: ACGAACGCGCCACTCTAT
Count the base differences between each pair of species and deduce which two species are most closely related. Calculate the percentage similarity for this pair and describe the cladogram these data support.
items.answer: species R–species S 1, species R–species P 4, species S–species P 3; species R and species S most closely related; 94.4 % similar; cladogram: species R and species S share a node, the third species branches off earlier
items.markingKey: Differences counted correctly (A1 for all three); fewest differences = most recent common ancestor: species R and species S (R1). (18 − 1)/18 × 100 = 94.4 % (A1); cladogram with closest pair as sister groups (A1).

items.stem: Explain how cladograms are constructed and evaluate their use in classification.
items.answer: Clade definition; shared derived characters; sequence alignment; count differences; parsimony; nodes = common ancestors; molecular clock for timing. Evaluation: objective, testable; reclassification (figworts, whales); limitations – convergence, rate variation, conflicting genes, hypotheses not facts.
items.markingKey: Clade definition; shared derived characters; sequence alignment; count differences; parsimony; nodes = common ancestors; molecular clock for timing. Evaluation: objective, testable; reclassification (figworts, whales); limitations – convergence, rate variation, conflicting genes, hypotheses not facts.

items.stem: Why is a mule not considered a species?
options: mules cannot survive in the wild
items.answer: mules are almost always infertile
items.markingKey: A. Horse × donkey hybrids cannot usually produce offspring.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "karyotype".
items.answer: The number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which molecule did Carl Woese compare to propose the three-domain system?
items.answer: ribosomal RNA
items.markingKey: ribosomal RNA. Woese sequenced 16S rRNA in the 1970s.

items.stem: Explain why cladograms are regarded as hypotheses rather than proven relationships.
items.answer: They are based on available data and assumptions (e.g. constant mutation rate, parsimony); different genes or methods can give different trees; new evidence may change them; they cannot be directly observed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are based on available data and assumptions (e.g. constant mutation rate, parsimony); different genes or methods can give different trees; new evidence may change them; they cannot be directly observed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why can eDNA give false negatives?
options: DNA degrades in the environment, especially with warmth and UV.
items.answer: DNA degrades in the environment, especially with warmth and UV.
items.markingKey: D. Degradation and dilution reduce detection.

items.stem: Distinguish between the biological species concept and the morphological species concept.
items.answer: The biological concept defines species by the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring; the morphological concept defines them by shared physical characteristics, which can be applied to fossils and asexual organisms but may mislead with dimorphism or cryptic species.
items.markingKey: The biological concept defines species by the ability to interbreed and produce fertile offspring; the morphological concept defines them by shared physical characteristics, which can be applied to fossils and asexual organisms but may mislead with dimorphism or cryptic species. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a karyogram is prepared and what it can show.
items.answer: Cells (e.g. lymphocytes or fetal cells) are stimulated to divide and stopped at metaphase; chromosomes are stained and photographed; homologues are paired by size, banding and centromere position; shows chromosome number, sex chromosomes and abnormalities such as trisomy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cells (e.g. lymphocytes or fetal cells) are stimulated to divide and stopped at metaphase; chromosomes are stained and photographed; homologues are paired by size, banding and centromere position; shows chromosome number, sex chromosomes and abnormalities such as trisomy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a natural classification and an artificial classification.
items.answer: An artificial classification groups organisms by convenient features (e.g. habitat or flight) that may be due to convergence; a natural classification groups organisms by common ancestry so groups are clades.
items.markingKey: An artificial classification groups organisms by convenient features (e.g. habitat or flight) that may be due to convergence; a natural classification groups organisms by common ancestry so groups are clades. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a traditional taxonomic group and a clade.
items.answer: A clade includes a common ancestor and all its descendants, defined by shared derived features or sequences; traditional groups may be based on overall similarity and can exclude some descendants (e.g. reptiles without birds).
items.markingKey: A clade includes a common ancestor and all its descendants, defined by shared derived features or sequences; traditional groups may be based on overall similarity and can exclude some descendants (e.g. reptiles without birds). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "An eDNA survey tells you exactly how many fish live in a lake." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: eDNA mainly shows presence/absence; the amount of DNA is only a rough indicator of abundance because it depends on shedding rates, degradation and water flow.
items.markingKey: eDNA mainly shows presence/absence; the amount of DNA is only a rough indicator of abundance because it depends on shedding rates, degradation and water flow. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the ring of Ensatina salamanders around the Central Valley of California as an example, explain the limitations of the biological species concept.
items.answer: Neighbouring populations interbreed, but the two end populations in the south coexist without interbreeding. Speciation is gradual, so there may be no clear point at which populations become separate species.
items.markingKey: Context (Neighbouring populations interbreed, but the two end populations in the south coexist without interbreeding.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Speciation is gradual, so there may be no clear point at which populations become separate species. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limitations of the biological species concept.

items.stem: A cell from a horse (2n = 64) and one from a donkey (2n = 62) produce gametes that fuse. What is the chromosome number of the mule?
items.markingKey: C. 32 + 31 = 63, unpaired chromosomes cause infertility.

items.stem: A gene accumulates about 1 base difference per 2 million years in each lineage. Two species differ at 30 bases. Approximately when did they diverge?
items.answer: 30 million years ago
items.markingKey: D. Differences accumulate in both lineages: 30 ÷ 2 lineages × 2 Myr = 30 Myr.

items.stem: Using the use of eDNA to track invasive Asian carp in the Great Lakes as an example, explain the benefits and limitations of eDNA.
items.answer: Carp DNA was detected beyond barriers, prompting further monitoring. It gives early warning of invasions but positive results may come from boats or birds carrying DNA, not live fish.
items.markingKey: Context (Carp DNA was detected beyond barriers, prompting further monitoring.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Whole-genome sequencing of every newborn baby should become routine."
items.answer: Targeted screening offers clear benefits now; routine whole-genome sequencing needs strong safeguards and better interpretation of variants before it is justified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it could detect genetic diseases early and guide treatment; costs have fallen dramatically. Arguments against: it raises issues of privacy, consent and possible discrimination; most variants are of uncertain significance and may cause anxiety. Supported judgement: Targeted screening offers clear benefits now; routine whole-genome sequencing needs strong safeguards and better interpretation of variants before it is justified.

items.stem: "The Linnaean hierarchy of ranks is no longer useful in modern biology." Discuss.
items.answer: Ranks remain useful as a communication tool, but classification should be based on clades revealed by molecular evidence; the hierarchy is a convention, not a natural law.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ranks (e.g. class, order) are arbitrary and not equivalent across groups; cladistics focuses on clades rather than ranks. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Molecular data should always take priority over morphological data when constructing cladograms."
items.answer: Molecular evidence is usually more reliable for living organisms, but the strongest cladograms combine molecular and morphological evidence, especially to include fossils.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sequences provide thousands of characters and are less affected by convergence; molecular data resolved relationships such as whales with hippos. Arguments against: DNA cannot be obtained from most fossils, so morphology is needed for extinct species; different genes can give conflicting trees, and horizontal gene transfer complicates analysis. Supported judgement: Molecular evidence is usually more reliable for living organisms, but the strongest cladograms combine molecular and morphological evidence, especially to include fossils. items.stem: "eDNA will soon make traditional field identification skills unnecessary." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: eDNA is a powerful complement, but field identification remains essential to validate results, build databases and study populations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: eDNA can detect many species quickly and cheaply, including rare and cryptic ones; metabarcoding can survey whole communities from one sample. Arguments against: eDNA gives little information on abundance, behaviour, condition or life stage; reference databases rely on specimens identified by trained taxonomists. Supported judgement: eDNA is a powerful complement, but field identification remains essential to validate results, build databases and study populations. items.stem: Define the term "binomial nomenclature".
items.answer: The system of naming each species with two Latin words, the genus name (capital) followed by the species name (lower case), printed in italics
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the system of naming each species with two Latin words, the genus name (capital) followed by the species name (lower case), printed in italics. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number and appearance of the chromosomes in a cell, arranged in homologous pairs in order of size and centromere position"?
items.answer: karyotype
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of karyotype.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The science of naming, describing and classifying organisms"?
items.answer: taxonomy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of taxonomy.

items.stem: Why can cladograms based on morphology be misleading?
options: Morphology is inherited directly from DNA in all cases.
Similar structures can arise by convergent evolution in unrelated groups.
Morphology is always better than DNA.
items.answer: Similar structures can arise by convergent evolution in unrelated groups.
items.markingKey: C. Analogous structures can mislead.

items.stem: Explain the difference between identification using DNA barcoding and identification using a dichotomous key.
items.answer: Keys use observable morphological features and need an intact specimen and expertise; barcoding compares a short DNA sequence with a database and can identify fragments, eggs or eDNA, but needs laboratory work and a complete reference library.
items.markingKey: Keys use observable morphological features and need an intact specimen and expertise; barcoding compares a short DNA sequence with a database and can identify fragments, eggs or eDNA, but needs laboratory work and a complete reference library. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which situation creates difficulty for the morphological species concept?
options: individuals that look similar and interbreed
a species with a binomial name
males and females of a species that look very different (sexual dimorphism)
populations living in the same area
items.answer: males and females of a species that look very different (sexual dimorphism)
items.markingKey: C. E.g. birds of paradise; also cryptic species that look alike but do not interbreed.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a karyotype and a genome.
items.answer: A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA.
items.markingKey: A karyotype describes the number and visible structure of chromosomes; a genome is the entire base sequence of the organism’s DNA. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why classification systems change over time.
items.answer: New evidence, especially DNA and protein sequences, can reveal that existing groups do not reflect common ancestry; organisms are reclassified (e.g. the creation of domains, the move of birds into a clade with reptiles); science is self-correcting.

items.stem: A student claims: "The more similar two species look, the more closely related they must be." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Similar appearance can result from convergent evolution; relationships are better shown by shared derived features and sequence data.
items.markingKey: Similar appearance can result from convergent evolution; relationships are better shown by shared derived features and sequence data. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Construct a dichotomous key to separate these four trees by their leaves: oak (simple, lobed), maple (simple, palmately lobed, opposite leaves), ash (compound, opposite leaflets), horse chestnut (compound, palmate). Describe the couplets.
items.answer: 1a leaf simple → 2; 1b leaf compound → 3. 2a lobes arranged palmately (from one point) → maple; 2b lobes along the midrib → oak. 3a leaflets arranged palmately from one point → horse chestnut; 3b leaflets in pairs along a central stalk → ash.

items.stem:
Cytochrome c is a protein of 104 amino acids found in the electron transport chain of all aerobic organisms. The table shows the number of amino acid differences between human cytochrome c and that of other species.

Species | Amino acid differences from human | % difference
rhesus monkey | 1 | 1.0
horse | 12 | 11.5
chicken | 13 | 12.5
rattlesnake | 14 | 13.5
yeast | 44 | ?

(a) Identify the species most closely related to humans according to these data. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage difference for yeast. [2]
(c) Explain why cytochrome c is useful for comparing distantly related species. [2]
(d) Explain how these data could be used to construct a cladogram. [2]
(e) Suggest why comparing DNA base sequences may give more information than comparing amino acid sequences. [2]
(f) Using a molecular clock of 1 amino acid change per 6 million years between lineages, estimate the time since humans and chicken shared a common ancestor. [1]
(g) Outline one limitation of using a single protein to deduce relationships. [1]
(h) Explain why the same protein can show differences between species despite having the same function. [2]
items.answer: (a) rhesus monkey (b) 42.3 % (c) It is found in all aerobic organisms (universal), has an essential function so changes slowly, so differences accumulate gradually over very long times. (d) Species with fewer differences share a more recent common ancestor and are placed on branches joined at a more recent node; the species with most differences branches off first (outgroup). (e) Because the code is degenerate, some base changes (silent mutations) do not change the amino acid; DNA also includes non-coding regions, so more differences can be detected. (f) 78 million years ago (g) Rates of change may vary between lineages; one protein gives few characters so trees may be unresolved or misleading; should be supported by other genes and fossils. (h) Mutations that do not affect the active regions are neutral and accumulate over time; more time since divergence means more differences.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] rhesus monkey (A1). (b) [2] 44/104 × 100 (M1) = 42.3 % (A1). (c) [2] Present in all aerobic organisms (A1); slow, steady rate of change (A1). (d) [2] Fewer differences = closer (A1); nodes as common ancestors / outgroup branching first (A1). (e) [2] Degenerate code / silent mutations (A1); more characters / non-coding DNA (A1). (f) [1] 13 × 6 = 78 Myr (A1); accept with assumption of constant rate. (g) [1] Any valid limitation (A1). (h) [2] Neutral mutations outside key regions (A1); accumulate with time (A1).
